title: Choose My Arts Challenge
objective: Use your own work and practical trials to choose a worthwhile arts-development challenge.

blocks.text: GROW · Art · Trinity Arts Award Silver. Choose My Arts Challenge.
Objective: Use your own work and practical trials to choose a worthwhile arts-development challenge.
Success evidence: Actual baseline work, an identified strength and development need, useful trial work and your own reasoned challenge choice.
Use your own artwork, interests and practical choices. You can choose an abstract subject; you do not need to disclose private experiences.
40 minutes. Keep original work before making changes. Ask staff about safe tools and access.

This deck directly serves Silver Unit 1, Part 1A, Plan an arts challenge. Silver has TWO units, evidenced separately. This lesson belongs to Unit 1, Arts practice and pathways; keep its evidence labelled by unit and part. ONE Attempted allowed PER UNIT. Any Not Attempted = Below Pass. The whole Silver portfolio has a 20-file cap, not twenty per unit or one new file per lesson. The four assessment areas are art form knowledge and understanding, creativity, planning and review, and communication. Results are Pass or Below Pass only. Only an adviser trained at Silver may assess; delivery is through a validated centre. Staff must confirm those conditions; neither is asserted as completed here. The arts challenge must not focus on leadership. Advisers must not write pupil plans, reviews or evidence. Prompt, read or scribe the pupil’s exact words and check them back unchanged. Core, Extend and Challenge vary support within Silver, retaining the same evidence expectation and the pupil’s own choices. Digital evidence is organised by unit and part, with every locator naming the actual filename plus page, slide or timecode. A portfolio structure is an option, not an extra award rule. Samples, trial counts and prompts here are teaching scaffolds, not qualification quotas. Use accessible tools and communication without forced personal disclosure, compulsory filming or public posting. This forty-minute lesson supports a longer programme of real guided and independent practice; it does not claim all award hours are complete. Source: tools/artsaward/SPEC.json, Silver and universal rules. This is the choice and self-assessment stage of 1A. The next deck supports the pupil’s own action plan. Prepare pencils, scrap paper, safe joining materials and examples the adult can make live; use the pupil’s actual work rather than an invented achievement profile. If no earlier work is available, a short piece made today becomes the honestly dated starting sample. The technique options are not pre-written challenges and do not require every pupil to make the same product. Staff demonstrate a feasible method, help the pupil examine evidence and arrange access; the pupil chooses the focus and intention.

stages.title: Arrival · retrieve
stages.data-ta1: Support a factual starting sample and a balanced view. Offer a close-up, spoken description or hands-on access; do not supply the pupil’s self-assessment.

blocks.text: Start with something you have made
Place a piece of your own art where you can examine it. A drawing, paper form or another piece can give you a starting point.
If no earlier piece is available, make a short sample today with the tools ready. Label it as today's starting work, rather than pretending it is older.
Find a part you can explain. What choice did you make, and what effect can you see?
A strength is something your work shows you can do. A weakness here means a skill that is not secure yet; it is not a judgement about you.
Point to evidence for both. Avoid choosing a weakness simply because someone else works in a different style.
Your challenge will grow from what you want your art to do next.

stages.title: Starter · create the need
stages.data-ta1: Invite discussion of artistic intention. Do not turn neatness, realism or a numerical score into a universal quality rule.

blocks.text: An interest needs a practical direction
You may know the kind of art you enjoy, yet still be unsure what to develop.
Saying that you like drawing does not identify a skill. Look more closely: are you interested in the weight of a line, a change of tone or the way shapes fill a space?
Paper work gives different questions. Do folds hold their shape? Does a join stay secure? How does the form change from another viewpoint?
Choose questions that matter to your own work. A bold, rough surface may be intentional; making everything neat is not the only useful direction.
Today you will test possibilities before choosing your challenge.

stages.title: I Do · model
stages.data-ta1: Make the tone patches live and leave the earlier patch visible. Narrate the evidence-to-choice method, without dictating a completed challenge for pupils.

blocks.text: Adult model: use a trial to discover a need
Watch the adult make a small tone study on scrap paper. This is their own demonstration, not a challenge you must copy.
They shade a light patch with the side of the pencil. They keep the hand relaxed and use overlapping strokes.
Next they build a darker patch with another light layer. They compare the two patches before pressing harder.
A sudden dark stripe appears where they stopped and restarted. The adult points to it and explains why it interrupts the gradual change they wanted.
They try overlapping the restart on a fresh patch. Now they can see whether that method better suits their intention.
The adult has evidence for a strength and a need: they can make different tones, while the transition needs more control.
Their next question comes from the work. They still have to decide whether this is the direction they want to pursue.
Your trial may reveal a different need. Perhaps a fold holds well but the join twists, or a repeated shape loses its rhythm.
Keep what the sample actually shows. Do not borrow the adult's judgement as your own.

blocks.title: Choose from work and practical evidence
blocks.caption: Look, try, compare and choose your direction.
blocks.alt: Four linked boxes move from examining actual work to testing a technique, comparing its effect and choosing a personal direction.

stages.title: We Do · everyone commits
stages.data-ta1: Suggested matches: A to 2, B to 3, C to 1. Accept reasoned alternatives. Keep all card text visible and ask pupils to relate options to their own work.

blocks.text: Visible technique cards: what could each help?
Match each technique to a possible effect. These are options to explore, not ready-made personal challenges.
Point to a match and explain how the action could affect the work. More than one effect may be possible.
Then select an option that connects with your baseline. You may propose another safe arts technique with staff support.

items: A · Build tone through light, overlapping pencil layers.
B · Fold a small foot at the bottom of a paper shape.
C · Change the spacing of a repeated mark.
1 · A different visual rhythm across the page.
3 · A form that can stand and be viewed from different sides.

stages.title: I Do 2 · connect
stages.data-ta1: Check feasibility and access without replacing the pupil’s intention. Distinguish a supported method from an adult-selected goal.

blocks.text: Choose a challenge with room to learn
A useful challenge is more than repeating the part you already find easy. It gives you an arts skill to develop and a reason for developing it.
It also needs to be possible with the time, tools and support available. An interesting idea can be made smaller without losing its purpose.
For example, you could explore a technique in a small study before deciding on a larger piece. The small study is a way to investigate, not a lower expectation.
Look at the adult’s trial beside their baseline. What changed when they used the technique? What remained difficult?
Think about the effect you want in your own artwork. Would this skill help you create it?
You do not need a perfect result today. You need an honest starting point and a direction worth exploring.
Keep alternatives until you have a reason to choose. A friend's preference can help you think, but it does not decide your challenge.

boxes.head: ALREADY SECURE
boxes.line1: a strength visible in my work
boxes.line2: something I can explain or repeat

boxes.head: WORTH DEVELOPING
boxes.line1: a skill linked to my intention
boxes.line2: something I can practise and check

blocks.title: Build from a strength towards a need
blocks.caption: Use both sides to choose a worthwhile challenge.
blocks.alt: Two panels place an evidenced strength beside a skill worth developing, supporting a personal challenge choice.

stages.title: We Do 2 · lab
stages.data-ta1: Teach the chosen safe technique before independent trials. Preserve separate samples rather than overwriting the only baseline. Capture an actual observation, not invented praise.

blocks.text: Try an option before you commit
Choose a suitable technique and make a small trial. You may compare another option if that will help your decision.
For tone, keep the first patch and try a different overlap beside it. For paper form, try a folded foot on scrap before joining a larger piece.
For a paper foot, fold a narrow strip at the base towards you. Press the crease, open the foot to a right angle and rest it on the table. Test whether the form stands before adding more weight.

For a repeated-mark trial, use one simple shape. Keep its size similar and change the spaces between marks across a short strip. Look at where the pattern feels steady and where it speeds up or pauses. Decide whether that rhythm suits the effect you want.
Look at the effect from the viewpoint that matters. A form should be checked from the side as well as from above.
Note what helped and what still needs work. A sketch, a spoken note or an arrow to the sample can record the finding.
Ask a partner or adult what they notice. Use their observation as another view, then make your own decision.

stages.title: Independent · evidence
stages.data-ta1: Scribe exactly or support an audio choice. Every tier retains the pupil’s own strength, development need, challenge, reason and actual starting evidence.

blocks.text: Choose your own challenge
Return to the baseline and the trial. Identify a strength and a skill you want to develop.
Now describe your chosen challenge in your own words. Explain what you want to explore or achieve in your art, and why this matters to you as a maker.
Use a detail from the work to support your reason. Avoid a target that just copies the adult model or a friend's idea.
Check that the materials and support are realistic. If they are not, adjust the scale or discuss another method while keeping your artistic intention.
Keep the baseline, trial and choice together under Unit 1, Part 1A. Add the actual filename and page, slide or timecode.

items: Core · use prompts to point, speak or write about your actual work. Identify your own strength and a skill to develop, try a suitable technique, then choose your challenge and reason. Keep the baseline and choice with an exact evidence location.

Extend · compare suitable techniques and choose the challenge in your own words. Explain how your trials and baseline support the choice. Keep the same strength, development need, reason and evidence.
Challenge · keep the same evidence and own choice. Compare the likely effect of two feasible directions, then explain which is more worthwhile for your arts practice and why.

stages.title: Exit · Audience and Influence
stages.data-ta1: Check that the choice is genuinely pupil-owned and feasible. Record a practical next step rather than awarding completion from a persuasive explanation alone.

blocks.text: Explain why this direction is yours
Show your chosen direction to someone who can see the work. Point to the detail that helped you decide.
Say what remains uncertain. You may need to test a material or find a manageable way to practise.
Keep that question with the challenge. Next time you will use it to build your own action plan.
The decision belongs to you. The work beside it helps another person understand how you reached it.

print.intro: Use your own work and a practical trial to choose an arts-development challenge. Keep the strength, development need and reason in your own words.
focusRows: What does my baseline show I can do, and what is not secure yet?
Which technique did I try, and what effect did it have?
What challenge do I choose, and why does it fit my artistic intention?
Is it feasible, and where are the baseline, trial and choice saved?
tiers: Core · use prompts to point, speak or write about your actual work. Identify your own strength and a skill to develop, try a suitable technique, then choose your challenge and reason. Keep the baseline and choice with an exact evidence location.

Extend · compare suitable techniques and choose the challenge in your own words. Explain how your trials and baseline support the choice. Keep the same strength, development need, reason and evidence.
Challenge · keep the same evidence and own choice. Compare the likely effect of two feasible directions, then explain which is more worthwhile for your arts practice and why.
checks: The starting work is real and its origin or date is recorded honestly.
My strength and development need are supported by details in the work.
A practical technique trial helped inform the choice.
The challenge and reason are my own and concern my arts development.
The work is labelled Unit 1, Part 1A with filename plus page, slide or timecode.
